title: Andhra to Enact Investment Protection Act So Deals Survive Regime Change
excerpt: Naidu told the CII summit that land, incentives and approvals granted to investors will be legally protected from reversal by future governments, with a Bill planned for the December winter session.
body:
• Andhra Pradesh will enact an Investment Protection Act so land allotments, incentives and approvals granted to investors cannot be arbitrarily reversed by a future government, Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu announced.
  • The Bill is planned for the Assembly's winter session in December; after passage it will be sent to the Centre, and Naidu has urged a similar national law.
  • The state has also launched escrow accounts for industrial incentives, so promised incentive money is set aside rather than dependent on future budgets.
  • At the CII summit, Naidu said 303 MoUs worth a proposed Rs 9.89 lakh crore would be signed; since June 2024 the state claims Rs 32.49 lakh crore in total investment proposals.

Andhra Pradesh will bring in an Investment Protection Act to stop future governments from cancelling the deals the current one signs. Announcing the proposal at the inaugural session of the 31st CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam on November 12, Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said the law would safeguard investors from regime changes and what he described as political vendetta, IANS reported. He urged the Union government to enact a similar law nationally.

What the Act would protect

Under the proposal, as Naidu described it to The Economic Times ahead of the summit and at the summit itself, the extent and place of land allotted, the incentives assured, and the permissions and approvals granted to an investor could not be changed by a successor government. Naidu called the framework a sovereign guarantee: a commitment made by one government would bind the next. The state has prepared a concept note to circulate to investors for feedback, and Naidu said he would introduce the Bill in the Assembly's winter session in December and send it to the Centre after passage. He has discussed the proposal with Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and urged him to take up a national version.

"I am bringing the Investment Protection Act. This will ensure if anyone invests in the state, no future government can change it."

— N. Chandrababu Naidu, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister

Escrow accounts come first

The Act has a practical companion already live. The state government has launched escrow accounts for industrial and investment incentives, The Hindu BusinessLine reported — meaning incentive money owed to a company is parked in a dedicated account rather than left to a future administration's budget choices. IT and HRD Minister Nara Lokesh said that after pioneering escrow accounts, Andhra Pradesh would be the first state in India to enact such an investor-protection law.

The numbers behind the pitch

The announcement was timed for the summit. Naidu said 303 MoUs involving proposed investments of Rs 9.89 lakh crore would be signed at the event, taking total investment proposals attracted since June 2024 to Rs 32.49 lakh crore. Lokesh gave a more granular conversion account: investment commitments worth Rs 22.6 lakh crore since June 2024, of which 73% had been converted into approved projects worth Rs 17.2 lakh crore, with 51% reaching ground-level implementation and projects worth Rs 5.9 lakh crore under construction. Those are the government's own figures, stated at the summit; MoUs and proposals are not grounded investment until projects are built.

Why investors care — and the open question

Policy reversal after a change of government is a standing complaint of large investors in India, and Andhra Pradesh's own recent history — projects reviewed or cancelled after the 2019 change of government — is the unspoken context of this law. The open question is legal design: how a state statute binds a future legislature, and what happens where a protected deal conflicts with environmental or public-interest obligations. Those answers will only come with the draft Bill in December. For now, the commitment is political and directional — and for NRI and diaspora investors weighing Andhra against other states, the escrow accounts are the part already in force.
